results.claim: For d=δ⁺(D)≥1, a directed cycle of length at least d+1 can be found in polynomial time; additionally, n<d+k is an immediate sound NO condition. Thus the target is completely solved for k=1.
results.proof_sketch: Greedily extend a simple directed path P=v₁…v_p until v_p has no out-neighbor outside P. All at least d out-neighbors of v_p therefore occur among v₁,…,v_{p−1}. If v_i is the earliest one, then d≤p−i, and v_i→v_{i+1}→…→v_p→v_i is a directed cycle on p−i+1≥d+1 vertices. The construction is polynomial. Conversely, no cycle has more than n vertices, so n<d+k certifies NO.

results.claim: For any integer L≥2, existence of a directed cycle of length at least L is exactly equivalent to a short-leg two-way linkage, yielding an explicit O(n^L(n+m)) exact algorithm.
results.proof_sketch: Enumerate every ordered L-tuple P=(v₁,…,v_L) of distinct vertices whose consecutive pairs are arcs. Delete v₂,…,v_{L−1} and test whether v_L reaches v₁. A simple return path together with P is a simple directed cycle of length at least L. Conversely, from any cycle of length at least L, take L consecutive vertices for P; the complementary segment is a return path avoiding P's internal vertices. Hence enumeration plus reachability is exact. For the target take L=d+k. This exposes the algorithmic bottleneck: the exponent depends on d+k, so this is not FPT in k.

results.claim: There is a polynomially checkable upper-bound certificate: if X is an independent vertex set and every arc entering X from outside X has its tail in S⊆V(D)\X, then every directed cycle has length at most n−|X|+|S|.
results.proof_sketch: For every x∈X lying on a directed cycle C, its predecessor on C cannot lie in X, since X is independent. By the entering-arc hypothesis that predecessor lies in S. Distinct vertices of C∩X have distinct predecessors, because a cycle vertex has only one successor on C. Thus |C∩X|≤|C∩S|≤|S|. At most n−|X| other vertices occur, proving |C|≤n−|X|+|S|. Therefore n−|X|+|S|<d+k is a verifiable NO certificate.

results.claim: For every fixed k≥4 there are 2-strong NO-instances with arbitrarily large minimum outdegree and with n≥d+k; indeed their circumference is exactly d+3.
results.proof_sketch: Let Q be a q-vertex set, q≥3, containing x,y, and let A be an a-vertex set, a≥2. Make Q complete bidirected; add every arc A→Q and every arc {x,y}→A; add no others. Deleting any vertex leaves a strong digraph: the surviving core is complete, every A-vertex reaches it, and at least one of x,y remains to reach all of A. Hence the digraph is 2-strong. Vertices in Q\{x,y} have outdegree q−1, vertices of A have outdegree q, so d=q−1. Every A-vertex on a cycle must be preceded by x or y, so a cycle contains at most two A-vertices and has length at most q+2. For distinct a₁,a₂∈A and an ordering z₁,…,z_{q−2} of Q\{x,y}, the cycle x,a₁,z₁,…,z_{q−2},y,a₂,x has length q+2. Thus the circumference is q+2=d+3. Taking a≥k−1 gives n≥d+k but no cycle of length d+k for k≥4. Consequently, neither large d nor a bounded number of vertices outside a longest cycle can supply the required FPT win condition.

results.claim: The target has a polynomial-time solution on semicomplete digraphs: such an input is YES exactly when n≥d+k, and a Hamiltonian directed cycle can be constructed when YES.
results.proof_sketch: A semicomplete digraph has at least one arc between every pair. Start with any directed cycle C in the strong input. If an outside vertex z satisfies c_i→z→c_{i+1} for consecutive vertices of C, insert z. If no such insertion exists, scanning cyclically shows every outside z either is dominated by every vertex of C and has no arc to C, or dominates every vertex of C and receives no arc from C: if both kinds of adjacency occurred, a transition around C would give an insertion. Strongness ensures both classes occur and supplies an arc u→v from the C-dominated class to the C-dominating class (take the first class transition on a path to C). Then replace any edge c_i→c_{i+1} by c_i→u→v→c_{i+1}. Repeating constructs a Hamiltonian cycle in polynomial time. A 2-strong digraph is strong, so the result applies. The size condition is necessary and sufficient.

final_writeup:
Let d=δ⁺(D) and n=|V(D)|, with 2-strong meaning that deleting any one vertex leaves a strong digraph. I did not obtain the required f(k)n^{O(1)} algorithm, so the resolution is partial.

The basic d+1 guarantee is constructive, and the target is trivial when k=1 or impossible when n<d+k. For a general threshold L, the problem admits an exact path-plus-return formulation: guess an L-vertex directed path and test for a return path avoiding its internal vertices. This gives a clean exact algorithm, but its n^L dependence becomes n^{d+k} here and therefore does not establish FPT in k.

A substantial obstruction to the usual large-degree win–win strategy is the explicit 2-strong family above. For every k≥4 it supplies arbitrarily large d and arbitrarily large n−(d+k), yet its longest cycle has only d+3 vertices. In particular, 2-strongness does not imply a bound such as min(n,2d): choosing q≥5 and a≥q−2 makes n≥2d while the circumference q+2 is smaller than 2d. The independent-set bottleneck lemma gives a short, polynomially verifiable certificate for these and related NO-instances.

On the positive side, the complete target is polynomial-time solvable for semicomplete inputs through a constructive Hamiltonicity argument. The unresolved general case must therefore handle sparse ordered pairs and large independent bottlenecks while avoiding an exponent depending on d.
checks_performed: Using exact Boolean reachability and Held–Karp subset dynamic programming, checked 16 members of the obstruction family with 3≤q≤6 and 2≤a≤5. Every deletion was strong, δ⁺=q−1, and the exact circumference was q+2.
Exhaustively enumerated all 3^10=59,049 labelled semicomplete digraphs on five vertices. All 51,969 strong instances had exact circumference five.
Exhaustively enumerated all 2^12=4,096 loopless digraphs on four vertices and thresholds L=2,3,4. In all 12,288 cases, the path-plus-return condition agreed with the exact circumference test.

All computations were in-memory and used exact integer/Boolean operations. The requested temporary directory could not be created because the filesystem was read-only; no repository files were modified.
